claim: Both unexpected pain and unexpected pain absence can drive avoidance learning.
source: Both unexpected pain and unexpected pain absence can drive avoidance learning, but whether they do so via shared or separate neural and neurochemical systems is largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the research question.

claim: Computational modeling provided evidence that untreated participants learned more from received than avoided pain.
source: Computational modeling provided evidence that untreated participants learned more from received than avoided pain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Dopamine manipulations negated the learning asymmetry by selectively increasing learning rates for avoided pain.
source: Our dopamine and opioid manipulations negated this learning asymmetry by selectively increasing learning rates for avoided pain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis comparing drug groups to placebo.

claim: Opioid manipulations negated the learning asymmetry by selectively increasing learning rates for avoided pain.
source: Our dopamine and opioid manipulations negated this learning asymmetry by selectively increasing learning rates for avoided pain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis comparing drug groups to placebo.

claim: Pain prediction errors were encoded in subcortical and limbic brain regions.
source: Furthermore, our fMRI analyses revealed that pain prediction errors were encoded in subcortical and limbic brain regions, whereas no-pain prediction errors were encoded in frontal and parietal cortical regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: No-pain prediction errors were encoded in frontal and parietal cortical regions.
source: Furthermore, our fMRI analyses revealed that pain prediction errors were encoded in subcortical and limbic brain regions, whereas no-pain prediction errors were encoded in frontal and parietal cortical regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: No effects of pharmacological manipulations on the neural encoding of prediction errors were found.
source: However, we found no effects of our pharmacological manipulations on the neural encoding of prediction errors.
evidence: This is a null finding from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Human pain-avoidance learning is supported by separate threat- and safety-learning systems.
source: Together, our results suggest that human pain-avoidance learning is supported by separate threat- and safety-learning systems, and that dopamine and endogenous opioids specifically regulate learning from successfully avoided pain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined behavioral and fMRI findings.

claim: Dopamine specifically regulates learning from successfully avoided pain.
source: Together, our results suggest that human pain-avoidance learning is supported by separate threat- and safety-learning systems, and that dopamine and endogenous opioids specifically regulate learning from successfully avoided pain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the drug effects on learning rates for avoided pain.

claim: Endogenous opioids specifically regulate learning from successfully avoided pain.
source: Together, our results suggest that human pain-avoidance learning is supported by separate threat- and safety-learning systems, and that dopamine and endogenous opioids specifically regulate learning from successfully avoided pain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the drug effects on learning rates for avoided pain.

claim: The experience of pain is an important teaching signal in avoidance learning.
source: The experience of pain is an important teaching signal in this learning process, such as when a child learns to avoid touching a hot stove, or when a patient who underwent knee surgery learns to avoid bending his or her knee.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The absence of otherwise expected pain can be an equally important teaching signal.
source: However, the absence of otherwise expected pain can be an equally important teaching signal.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Previous studies have made considerable progress in understanding the neural basis of passive cue–pain association learning.
source: Previous studies have made considerable progress in our understanding of the neural basis of passive cue–pain association learning (Ploghaus et al., 2000; Seymour et al., 2004; Seymour et al., 2005) and—more recently—active pain-avoidance and -relief learning (Roy et al., 2014; Eldar et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies have made considerable progress in understanding the neural basis of active pain-avoidance and -relief learning.
source: Previous studies have made considerable progress in our understanding of the neural basis of passive cue–pain association learning (Ploghaus et al., 2000; Seymour et al., 2004; Seymour et al., 2005) and—more recently—active pain-avoidance and -relief learning (Roy et al., 2014; Eldar et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: According to reinforcement-learning theory, learning is driven by prediction errors.
source: According to reinforcement-learning theory, learning is driven by prediction errors, which signal the difference between the actual and expected outcomes of an action (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from reinforcement learning theory, supported by citation.

claim: Prediction errors signal the difference between the actual and expected outcomes of an action.
source: According to reinforcement-learning theory, learning is driven by prediction errors, which signal the difference between the actual and expected outcomes of an action (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from reinforcement learning theory, supported by citation.

claim: Actions that result in the unexpected presence of pain yield positively signed prediction errors which increase the aversive value associated with that action.
source: Thus, actions that result in the unexpected presence vs. absence of pain yield oppositely signed prediction errors which, respectively, increase and decrease the aversive value associated with that action.
evidence: This is an inference from reinforcement learning theory applied to pain-avoidance learning.

claim: Actions that result in the unexpected absence of pain yield negatively signed prediction errors which decrease the aversive value associated with that action.
source: Thus, actions that result in the unexpected presence vs. absence of pain yield oppositely signed prediction errors which, respectively, increase and decrease the aversive value associated with that action.
evidence: This is an inference from reinforcement learning theory applied to pain-avoidance learning.

claim: A previous fMRI study identified brain activity encoding general aversive prediction errors.
source: For example, in a previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study, we identified brain activity encoding general aversive prediction errors, signaling the degree to which both received- and avoided-pain outcomes are relatively worse (or less good) than expected (Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: There is a wealth of evidence that reward prediction errors are signaled by phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: Regarding the role of neuromodulators, there is a wealth of evidence that reward prediction errors, which are thought to drive reward-pursuit behaviors, are signaled by phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons (Schultz et al., 1997) that project to the ventral striatum (O'Doherty et al., 2003, Rutledge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons project to the ventral striatum.
source: Regarding the role of neuromodulators, there is a wealth of evidence that reward prediction errors, which are thought to drive reward-pursuit behaviors, are signaled by phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons (Schultz et al., 1997) that project to the ventral striatum (O'Doherty et al., 2003, Rutledge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Unexpected rewards trigger a phasic increase (burst) in dopamine activity.
source: Specifically, unexpected rewards trigger a phasic increase (burst) in dopamine activity, while the unexpected absence of reward triggers a phasic decrease (dip) in dopamine activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dopamine signaling.

claim: The unexpected absence of reward triggers a phasic decrease (dip) in dopamine activity.
source: Specifically, unexpected rewards trigger a phasic increase (burst) in dopamine activity, while the unexpected absence of reward triggers a phasic decrease (dip) in dopamine activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dopamine signaling.

claim: Whether the dopamine system has a role in aversive learning is controversial.
source: Whether the dopamine system also has a role in aversive learning is controversial, but several hypotheses have been proposed, mostly based on animal studies (Palminteri and Pessiglione, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as current state of knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: According to one prominent account, the same dopaminergic prediction-error response that reinforces actions associated with reward also reinforces actions associated with the omission of aversive outcomes.
source: According to one prominent account, the same dopaminergic prediction-error response that reinforces actions associated with reward also reinforces actions associated with the omission of aversive outcomes (Mowrer, 1956; Dinsmoor, 2001; Moutoussis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical account supported by citations.

claim: Animal studies have provided mixed evidence for the idea that dopamine bursts support learning from successfully avoided pain.
source: However, animal studies have provided mixed evidence for this idea (Josselyn et al., 2005; Oleson et al., 2012; Wietzikoski et al., 2012; Dombrowski et al., 2013; Fernando et al., 2013; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Wenzel et al., 2018; Stelly et al., 2019) and evidence in humans is scarce (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Evidence in humans for dopamine bursts supporting learning from successfully avoided pain is scarce.
source: However, animal studies have provided mixed evidence for this idea (Josselyn et al., 2005; Oleson et al., 2012; Wietzikoski et al., 2012; Dombrowski et al., 2013; Fernando et al., 2013; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Wenzel et al., 2018; Stelly et al., 2019) and evidence in humans is scarce (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citation.

claim: It has been proposed that negative punishment learning is mediated by phasic dips or pauses in dopamine activity, via an effect on D2 receptors.
source: In addition, it has been proposed that negative punishment learning is mediated by phasic dips or pauses in dopamine activity, via an effect on D2 receptors (Frank, 2005; Maia and Frank, 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Pavlovian fear conditioning studies in animals have provided evidence for a causal role of opioidergic activity in fear conditioning.
source: Pavlovian fear conditioning studies in animals have provided evidence for a causal role of opioidergic activity—specifically via μ-opioid receptors in the periaqueductal gray (PAG)—in both fear conditioning (McNally and Cole, 2006; Cole and McNally, 2007; Cole and McNally, 2009; McNally et al., 2011) and fear-extinction learning (McNally and Westbrook, 2003; McNally et al., 2004; McNally et al., 2005; Kim and Richardson, 2009; Parsons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Pavlovian fear conditioning studies in animals have provided evidence for a causal role of opioidergic activity in fear-extinction learning.
source: Pavlovian fear conditioning studies in animals have provided evidence for a causal role of opioidergic activity—specifically via μ-opioid receptors in the periaqueductal gray (PAG)—in both fear conditioning (McNally and Cole, 2006; Cole and McNally, 2007; Cole and McNally, 2009; McNally et al., 2011) and fear-extinction learning (McNally and Westbrook, 2003; McNally et al., 2004; McNally et al., 2005; Kim and Richardson, 2009; Parsons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Opioidergic activity in fear conditioning and extinction learning is specifically via μ-opioid receptors in the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: Pavlovian fear conditioning studies in animals have provided evidence for a causal role of opioidergic activity—specifically via μ-opioid receptors in the periaqueductal gray (PAG)—in both fear conditioning (McNally and Cole, 2006; Cole and McNally, 2007; Cole and McNally, 2009; McNally et al., 2011) and fear-extinction learning (McNally and Westbrook, 2003; McNally et al., 2004; McNally et al., 2005; Kim and Richardson, 2009; Parsons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: In humans, endogenous opioids are well known to mediate pain relief.
source: In humans, endogenous opioids are well known to mediate pain relief (Levine et al., 1978; Eippert et al., 2009) as well as pleasure and liking responses (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015; Nummenmaa and Tuominen, 2018), but it is currently unknown whether the roles of the opioid system in affective valuation also influence pain-related learning.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In humans, endogenous opioids are well known to mediate pleasure and liking responses.
source: In humans, endogenous opioids are well known to mediate pain relief (Levine et al., 1978; Eippert et al., 2009) as well as pleasure and liking responses (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015; Nummenmaa and Tuominen, 2018), but it is currently unknown whether the roles of the opioid system in affective valuation also influence pain-related learning.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It is currently unknown whether the roles of the opioid system in affective valuation also influence pain-related learning.
source: In humans, endogenous opioids are well known to mediate pain relief (Levine et al., 1978; Eippert et al., 2009) as well as pleasure and liking responses (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015; Nummenmaa and Tuominen, 2018), but it is currently unknown whether the roles of the opioid system in affective valuation also influence pain-related learning.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Participants completed the learning task under one of three drug conditions: 100 mg levodopa, 50 mg naltrexone, or placebo.
source: Specifically, participants completed the learning task under one of three drug conditions: 100 mg levodopa (a dopamine precursor), 50 mg naltrexone (an opioid antagonist, with highest affinity for the μ-opioid receptor), or placebo.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Levodopa is a dopamine precursor.
source: Specifically, participants completed the learning task under one of three drug conditions: 100 mg levodopa (a dopamine precursor), 50 mg naltrexone (an opioid antagonist, with highest affinity for the μ-opioid receptor), or placebo.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist, with highest affinity for the μ-opioid receptor.
source: Specifically, participants completed the learning task under one of three drug conditions: 100 mg levodopa (a dopamine precursor), 50 mg naltrexone (an opioid antagonist, with highest affinity for the μ-opioid receptor), or placebo.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: PET studies in humans suggest that levodopa increases phasic dopamine bursts.
source: PET studies in humans suggest that levodopa increases phasic dopamine bursts (Floel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Naltrexone blocks the majority of μ-opioid receptors in the brain.
source: Naltrexone blocks the majority of μ-opioid receptors in the brain (Lee et al., 1988; Preston and Bigelow, 1993; Schuh et al., 1999; Weerts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Eighty-three healthy human participants completed a pain-avoidance learning task during fMRI.
source: Eighty-three healthy human participants completed a pain-avoidance learning task during fMRI, under one of three treatment conditions (levodopa, naltrexone, or placebo).
evidence: This describes the study sample and design.

claim: On each trial of the pain-avoidance learning task, participants chose between two options, each probabilistically associated with the delivery of painful heat.
source: On each of 144 trials of the pain-avoidance learning task, participants chose between two options (Figure 1A), each probabilistically associated with the delivery of painful heat (49 or 50°C, 1.9 s duration) to their left lower leg.
evidence: This describes the task design, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Pain probabilities for each option were governed by two independently varying random walks.
source: Pain probabilities for each option were governed by two independently varying random walks (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the task design, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: There were no treatment effects on subjective state (alertness, calmness, or contentment).
source: There were no treatment effects on subjective state (alertness, calmness, or contentment; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or self-reported heat pain during a separate pain-rating task immediately preceding the avoidance-learning task (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a null finding from the subjective state measures, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no treatment effects on self-reported heat pain during a separate pain-rating task immediately preceding the avoidance-learning task.
source: There were no treatment effects on subjective state (alertness, calmness, or contentment; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or self-reported heat pain during a separate pain-rating task immediately preceding the avoidance-learning task (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a null finding from the pain-rating task, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nine participants were excluded from the fMRI analyses because of excessive head movement.
source: Nine participants were excluded from the fMRI (but not the behavioral) analyses because of excessive head movement.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the fMRI analyses.

claim: The behavioral analyses included 83 participants (26–29 per treatment group).
source: Thus, the behavioral analyses included 83 participants (26–29 per treatment group), and the fMRI analyses included 74 participants (24–26 per treatment group).
evidence: This describes the final sample size for behavioral analyses.

claim: The fMRI analyses included 74 participants (24–26 per treatment group).
source: Thus, the behavioral analyses included 83 participants (26–29 per treatment group), and the fMRI analyses included 74 participants (24–26 per treatment group).
evidence: This describes the final sample size for fMRI analyses.

claim: On average, participants received pain on 57.1 of the 144 trials (standard deviation = 8.6).
source: On average, participants received pain on 57.1 of the 144 trials (standard deviation [SD] = 8.6).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: Participants switched to the other choice option more frequently after receiving pain (46.6% of those trials) than after avoiding pain (5.4% of those trials).
source: As expected, participants switched to the other choice option more frequently after receiving pain (46.6% of those trials, SD = 21.2) than after avoiding pain (5.4% of those trials, SD = 6.9; t(82) = 18.6, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.0).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis with statistical support.

claim: The effect of previous pain outcomes on switching decayed exponentially over time, in all treatment groups.
source: The effect of previous pain outcomes on switching also decayed exponentially over time, in all treatment groups (Figure 1C; p < 0.001, Cohen's d > 2.2 for 1 trial back, p < 0.002, Cohen's d > 0.7 for 2 trials back, and p > 0.047, Cohen's d < 0.4 for 3–6 trials back, in all groups).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis with statistical support, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations did not affect basic measures of task performance.
source: Thus, our pharmacological manipulations did not affect basic measures of task performance.
evidence: This is an inference from the null findings on switching behavior and number of pain outcomes.

claim: Choice reaction times were faster when participants stayed with the same choice option following a no-pain outcome than when participants either stayed or switched following a pain outcome.
source: Choice reaction times (RTs) were faster when participants stayed with the same choice option following a no-pain outcome (no pain/stay choices; mean = 729 ms) than when participants either stayed or switched following a pain outcome (mean = 778 and 795, respectively; no pain/stay vs. pain/stay: t(82) = 5.0, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.54; no pain/stay vs. pain/switch: t(82) = 6.9, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.76).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis with statistical support.

claim: In all treatment groups, the model with separate learning rates for received and avoided pain (Model 2) outperformed the model with a single learning rate (Model 1).
source: In all treatment groups, the model with separate learning rates for received and avoided pain (Model 2) outperformed the model with a single learning rate (Model 1), providing initial evidence for the presence of two learning systems.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis based on model comparison.

claim: The WAIC for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 3109 vs. 2959 for the placebo group.
source: The Watanabe–Akaike information criterion (WAIC) for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 3109 vs. 2959, 2958 vs. 2941, and 3164 vs. 3106 for the placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone groups, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model comparison.

claim: The WAIC for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 2958 vs. 2941 for the levodopa group.
source: The Watanabe–Akaike information criterion (WAIC) for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 3109 vs. 2959, 2958 vs. 2941, and 3164 vs. 3106 for the placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone groups, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model comparison.

claim: The WAIC for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 3164 vs. 3106 for the naltrexone group.
source: The Watanabe–Akaike information criterion (WAIC) for Model 1 vs. Model 2 was 3109 vs. 2959, 2958 vs. 2941, and 3164 vs. 3106 for the placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone groups, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model comparison.

claim: Both levodopa and naltrexone, as compared to placebo, increased learning rates for avoided pain, while not affecting learning from received pain.
source: Thus, at the group level, both levodopa and naltrexone, as compared to placebo, increased learning rates for avoided pain, while not affecting learning from received pain (Figure 2A, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis comparing drug groups to placebo, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Participants in the two drug groups, as compared to the placebo group, were less prone to choose the option with the lowest expected pain probability (i.e., more stochastic choice behavior).
source: This suggests that participants in the two drug groups, as compared to the placebo group, were less prone to choose the option with the lowest expected pain probability (i.e., more stochastic choice behavior).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lower inverse-temperature parameter in the drug groups.

claim: The modeling procedure was able to correctly recover the simulated parameters.
source: In sum, our modeling procedure was able to correctly recover the simulated parameters, suggesting that it is unlikely that the parameters observed in the different pharmacological-manipulation conditions are artifacts of our parameter-optimization procedure.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter-recovery analysis.

claim: The simulated datasets produced similar model-independent performance measures in the drug and placebo groups, despite the fact that the simulated choices were produced by different sets of parameters.
source: Moreover, the simulated datasets also produced similar model-independent performance measures (number of received pain stimuli, switch frequencies) in the drug and placebo groups, despite the fact that the simulated choices were produced by different sets of parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from the data simulation analysis.

claim: Levodopa and naltrexone really had two computational effects—an increased learning rate for avoided pain, and an increased degree of choice stochasticity—which combination yielded no significant effects on model-independent performance measures.
source: These findings suggest that levodopa and naltrexone really had two computational effects—an increased learning rate for avoided pain, and an increased degree of choice stochasticity—which combination yielded no significant effects on model-independent performance measures.
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter-recovery and data simulation analyses.

claim: Regions encoding the unexpectedness or surprise evoked by received pain should respond stronger to pain outcomes when pain was less expected.
source: Regions encoding the unexpectedness or surprise evoked by received pain should respond stronger to pain outcomes when pain was less expected (i.e., a negative correlation with expected pain probability on pain trials).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction for the fMRI analysis.

claim: Regions encoding the surprise evoked by avoided pain should respond stronger to no-pain outcomes when pain was more expected.
source: In contrast, regions encoding the surprise evoked by avoided pain should respond stronger to no-pain outcomes when pain was more expected (i.e., a positive correlation with expected pain probability on no-pain trials; Figure 3A, left plots).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction for the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The contrast 'negative correlation with expected pain probability on pain trials > positive correlation with expected pain probability on no-pain trials' revealed activation in the vmPFC and rostral ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, insula extending into the left parahippocampal gyrus, cerebellum, and a brainstem region encompassing part of the PAG.
source: This contrast revealed activation in the vmPFC and rostral ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, insula extending into the left parahippocampal gyrus, cerebellum, and a brainstem region encompassing part of the PAG (Figure 3A, yellow regions).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Extensive clusters showed positive correlation with expected pain probability on no-pain trials > negative correlation with expected pain probability on pain trials in sensorimotor cortex, parietal and occipital cortex, and the bilateral frontal poles.
source: We also found extensive clusters that showed the opposite effect—that is positive correlation with expected pain probability on no-pain trials > negative correlation with expected pain probability on pain trials—in sensorimotor cortex, parietal and occipital cortex, and the bilateral frontal poles (Figure 3A, blue regions), suggesting that these regions show a stronger surprise response for avoided than received pain.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The contrast for absolute prediction errors revealed extensive activation clusters in the dorsal ACC extending into the supplementary motor cortex, insula, sensorimotor cortex, thalamus, part of the brainstem and cerebellum.
source: This contrast revealed extensive activation clusters in the dorsal ACC extending into the supplementary motor cortex, insula, sensorimotor cortex, thalamus, part of the brainstem and cerebellum, suggesting that these regions encoded absolute prediction error (Figure 3B, yellow regions).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: A few smaller clusters in left sensorimotor cortex, right dlPFC, and left frontopolar cortex showed the opposite effect, suggesting that these regions encoded the overall expectedness of outcomes.
source: In addition, a few smaller clusters in left sensorimotor cortex, right dlPFC, and left frontopolar cortex showed the opposite effect, suggesting that these regions encoded the overall expectedness of outcomes (Figure 3B, blue regions).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Positive activation for both contrasts (surprise more for received than avoided pain, and absolute prediction error) was found in a set of mostly subcortical and limbic regions, including a large cluster in the brainstem, bilateral insula extending into the amygdala, rostral ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, bilateral supramarginal gyrus, and cerebellum.
source: Positive activation for both contrasts was found in a set of mostly subcortical and limbic regions, including a large cluster in the brainstem (not covering the PAG), bilateral insula extending into the amygdala, rostral ACC, posterior cingulate cortex, bilateral supramarginal gyrus, and cerebellum (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the conjunction analysis of fMRI contrasts, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: These regions encoded surprise more for received than avoided pain (pain-specific prediction errors), which could not be explained by a general sensitivity to expected pain probability.
source: These regions thus encoded surprise more for received than avoided pain (pain-specific prediction errors), which could not be explained by a general sensitivity to expected pain probability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conjunction analysis results.

claim: Negative activation for the first contrast and positive activation for the second contrast was found in several cortical regions, including the supplementary motor cortex, left parietal cortex (supramarginal gyrus), bilateral somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), and left dlPFC (middle and superior frontal gyrus).
source: Negative activation for the first contrast and positive activation for the second contrast, on the other hand, was found in several cortical regions, including the supplementary motor cortex, left parietal cortex (supramarginal gyrus), bilateral somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), and left dlPFC (middle and superior frontal gyrus) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the conjunction analysis of fMRI contrasts, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: These regions encoded surprise more for avoided than received pain (no-pain-specific prediction errors), which could not be explained by a general sensitivity to expected pain probability.
source: These regions thus encoded surprise more for avoided than received pain (no-pain-specific prediction errors), which could not be explained by a general sensitivity to expected pain probability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conjunction analysis results.

claim: These results provide evidence that prediction errors evoked by pain and no-pain outcomes are encoded in largely distinct brain regions.
source: Together, these results provide evidence that prediction errors evoked by pain and no-pain outcomes are encoded in largely distinct brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference from the fMRI findings showing different brain regions for pain-specific and no-pain-specific prediction errors.

claim: No differences between the levodopa and placebo group, or between the naltrexone and placebo group, were found for any of the fMRI contrasts (whole-brain FDR corrected).
source: However, we found no differences between the levodopa and placebo group, or between the naltrexone and placebo group, for any of the contrasts reported above (whole-brain FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a null finding from the fMRI analysis comparing drug groups to placebo.

claim: The higher learning rate for pain than no-pain outcomes in the placebo group suggests that people normally update their expectations more following received than avoided pain.
source: The higher learning rate for pain than no-pain outcomes in the placebo group suggests that people normally (in the absence of a pharmacological manipulation) update their expectations more following received than avoided pain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling findings.

claim: A similar learning-rate asymmetry was found in a recent aversive reversal-learning study.
source: A similar learning-rate asymmetry was found in a recent aversive reversal-learning study (Wise et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reward-learning studies using secondary reinforcers have provided evidence for the opposite asymmetry: higher learning rates for favorable than unfavorable outcomes.
source: Interestingly, however, reward-learning studies using secondary reinforcers (e.g., monetary gains and losses) have provided evidence for the opposite asymmetry: higher learning rates for favorable than unfavorable outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: The opposite learning bias in reward-learning studies has been attributed to an optimistic learning bias.
source: This has been attributed to an optimistic learning bias (Sharot and Garrett, 2016; Lefebvre et al., 2017) and a tendency to learn preferentially from information that confirms one's current action (Palminteri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The opposite learning bias in reward-learning studies has been attributed to a tendency to learn preferentially from information that confirms one's current action.
source: This has been attributed to an optimistic learning bias (Sharot and Garrett, 2016; Lefebvre et al., 2017) and a tendency to learn preferentially from information that confirms one's current action (Palminteri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The opposite learning asymmetry in pain-avoidance learning tasks may be due to the intrinsically aversive nature of pain, arguably rendering unexpected pain a more salient teaching signal than unexpected pain absence.
source: The opposite learning bias in pain-avoidance learning tasks may be due to the intrinsically aversive nature of pain, arguably rendering unexpected pain a more salient teaching signal than unexpected pain absence.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed learning asymmetry.

claim: Higher learning rates for received than avoided pain may reflect a Pavlovian influence on choice which operates in parallel to the instrumental learning system.
source: Relatedly, the experience of pain may trigger a reflexive tendency to change one's course of action (Huys et al., 2012), expressed in elevated learning rates for pain outcomes. Thus, higher learning rates for received than avoided pain may reflect a Pavlovian influence on choice which operates in parallel to the instrumental learning system.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed learning asymmetry, with citation support.

claim: Levodopa and naltrexone selectively increased learning rates for successfully avoided pain, consistent with a role for dopamine and endogenous opioids in safety learning.
source: Levodopa and naltrexone selectively increased learning rates for successfully avoided pain, consistent with a role for dopamine and endogenous opioids in safety learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the drug effects on learning rates.

claim: Previous studies have associated levodopa-induced increases in phasic dopamine activity with enhanced learning from (secondary) rewards.
source: Previous studies have associated levodopa-induced increases in phasic dopamine activity with enhanced learning from (secondary) rewards (Frank et al., 2004; Pessiglione et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Combined with previous findings, the levodopa results suggest that phasic dopamine activity may signal the degree to which outcomes are 'better than expected' across both reward and punishment domains.
source: Combined with these previous findings, our levodopa results suggest that phasic dopamine activity may signal the degree to which outcomes are 'better than expected' across both reward and punishment domains.
evidence: This is an inference from the current findings combined with previous research.

claim: One previous study provided correlational evidence for a role of dopamine in human safety learning in a Pavlovian fear-conditioning task.
source: We are aware of one previous study that provided correlational evidence for a role of dopamine in human safety learning in a Pavlovian fear-conditioning task (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: That previous study found that individual differences in fear-extinction learning rates were associated with genetic variation in the dopamine transporter gene.
source: That study found that individual differences in fear-extinction learning rates were associated with genetic variation in the dopamine transporter gene, which presumably affects phasic striatal dopamine release.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous research.

claim: The levodopa results provide the first causal evidence for a role of dopamine in human safety learning in an instrumental learning task.
source: Our levodopa results are consistent with this result, and provide the first causal evidence for a role of dopamine in human safety learning in an instrumental learning task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The results do not support the idea that dopamine supports learning from aversive outcomes.
source: Levodopa did not affect learning rates for received pain; hence our results do not support the idea that dopamine supports learning from aversive outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference from the null effect of levodopa on learning rates for pain outcomes.

claim: The results suggest a selective role for the human dopamine system in learning from successfully avoided pain.
source: Instead, our results suggest a selective role for the human dopamine system in learning from successfully avoided pain.
evidence: This is an inference from the selective effect of levodopa on learning rates for avoided pain.

claim: Naltrexone increased learning rates for avoided pain, counterintuitively suggesting that μ-opioid activity normally suppresses learning from avoided pain.
source: However, we found the opposite effect for avoided-pain outcomes: like levodopa, naltrexone increased learning rates for avoided pain. This finding counterintuitively suggests that μ-opioid activity normally suppresses learning from avoided pain and that naltrexone countered this effect, which seems to contradict findings that μ-opioid-receptor antagonists impair fear-extinction learning in rats (McNally and Westbrook, 2003; McNally et al., 2004; McNally et al., 2005; Kim and Richardson, 2009; Parsons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the naltrexone findings, noting the apparent contradiction with previous animal studies.

claim: The levodopa and naltrexone groups showed a higher degree of choice stochasticity than the placebo group.
source: The levodopa and naltrexone groups also showed a higher degree of choice stochasticity than the placebo group, suggesting that participants in both drug groups were less prone to choose the option with the lowest expected pain probability.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The parameter-recovery analysis indicated that the drug effects on learning rate for avoided pain and choice stochasticity could be independently and correctly retrieved.
source: Importantly, our parameter-recovery analysis indicated that the drug effects on learning rate for avoided pain and choice stochasticity could be independently and correctly retrieved.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter-recovery analysis.

claim: The increased choice stochasticity in the levodopa group may reflect a positive association between dopamine activity and risk preference.
source: The increased choice stochasticity in the levodopa group may reflect a positive association between dopamine activity and risk preference (Voon et al., 2006; Gallagher et al., 2007; St Onge and Floresco, 2009; Chew et al., 2019) or exploration (Beeler et al., 2010; Kayser et al., 2015; Gershman and Tzovaras, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The increased choice stochasticity in the levodopa group may reflect a positive association between dopamine activity and exploration.
source: The increased choice stochasticity in the levodopa group may reflect a positive association between dopamine activity and risk preference (Voon et al., 2006; Gallagher et al., 2007; St Onge and Floresco, 2009; Chew et al., 2019) or exploration (Beeler et al., 2010; Kayser et al., 2015; Gershman and Tzovaras, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The increased choice stochasticity in the levodopa group is broadly consistent with recent evidence that levodopa reduces the impact of valence on information seeking.
source: It is also broadly consistent with recent evidence that levodopa reduces the impact of valence on information seeking (Vellani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pain-specific prediction errors were predominantly encoded in subcortical (brainstem, cerebellum) and limbic (insula, amygdala, rostral ACC) regions that are typically associated with emotional and affective processes.
source: Pain-specific prediction errors were predominantly encoded in subcortical (brainstem, cerebellum) and limbic (insula, amygdala, rostral ACC) regions that are typically associated with emotional and affective processes, including fear conditioning (Phillips and LeDoux, 1992) and affective responses to errors (Bush et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings, with citations to support the functional characterization of these regions.

claim: No-pain-specific prediction errors were encoded in frontal and parietal cortical areas typically associated with higher-order cognitive processing.
source: In contrast, no-pain-specific prediction errors were encoded in frontal and parietal cortical areas typically associated with higher-order cognitive processing (Ptak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings, with citation to support the functional characterization of these regions.

claim: Prediction errors for no-pain outcomes were not represented in the ventral striatum, which is typically found for reward prediction errors.
source: Prediction errors for no-pain outcomes were not represented in the ventral striatum, which is typically found for reward prediction errors (O'Doherty et al., 2003, Rutledge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI analysis, with citations to previous work on reward prediction errors.

claim: The frontoparietal activity for no-pain outcomes possibly reflected increased attention on trials in which pain was expected but not received.
source: Instead, prediction errors for no-pain outcomes were associated with frontoparietal activity. This activity is unlikely to reflect a reward signal, but possibly reflected increased attention on trials in which pain was expected but not received.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: The absence of a striatal 'reward-like' prediction-error response for no-pain outcomes suggests that, in terms of neural processing, learning from avoided pain is not comparable to learning from rewards.
source: The absence of a striatal 'reward-like' prediction-error response for no-pain outcomes suggests that, in terms of neural processing, learning from avoided pain is not comparable to learning from rewards.
evidence: This is an inference from the fMRI findings.

claim: The lack of a detectable reward-like prediction-error response may be related to the task design, in which pain outcomes involved a change in sensory input whereas no-pain outcomes did not.
source: However, the lack of a detectable reward-like prediction-error response may also be related to our task design. Specifically, pain outcomes in our task involved a change in sensory input (a rise in temperature) whereas no-pain outcomes did not (maintenance of the baseline temperature), which may have caused a more prominent neural prediction-error response for the pain outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the absence of striatal activation for no-pain outcomes.

claim: The stronger subcortical and limbic ('emotional') responses for pain than for no-pain prediction errors may foster a behavioral state that favors inactivity and rest, which could promote tissue healing and recovery.
source: It is an interesting speculation that, in such situations, the stronger subcortical and limbic ('emotional') responses for pain than for no-pain prediction errors, as found in our study, may foster a behavioral state that favors inactivity and rest, which could promote tissue healing and recovery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the fMRI findings.

claim: The absence of drug effects on fMRI activation may indicate that the dopamine and opioid systems are not involved in pain-avoidance learning, although this is inconsistent with the drug effects on learning rates for avoided pain.
source: Unexpectedly, we found no effects of levodopa or naltrexone on any of our fMRI prediction-error contrasts. This may indicate that the dopamine and opioid systems are not involved in pain-avoidance learning, although this is inconsistent with the drug effects on learning rates for avoided pain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null fMRI findings.

claim: It is possible that the pharmacological manipulations did affect prediction-error-related dopamine and/or opioid activity, but that there was not enough statistical power to detect these effects due to the moderate sample size and between-subject design.
source: It is also possible that our pharmacological manipulations did affect prediction-error-related dopamine and/or opioid activity, but that we did not have enough statistical power to detect these effects due to our moderate sample size and between-subject design (24–26 participants per treatment group).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the null fMRI findings.

claim: The absence of drug effects on fMRI activation at the group level may be explained by individual differences in drug responses.
source: The absence of drug effects on fMRI activation at the group level may also be explained by individual differences in drug responses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the null fMRI findings.

claim: Several studies have shown that effects of dopaminergic drugs on cognitive function depend on an individual's baseline level of performance or dopamine activity.
source: Several studies have shown that effects of dopaminergic drugs on cognitive function depend on an individual's baseline level of performance or dopamine activity reviewed in Cools and D'Esposito, 2011, Frank and Fossella, 2011, consistent with the idea that the relationship between dopamine activity and neurocognitive function follows an inverted U-shape function (Cools and Robbins, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relationship between dopamine activity and neurocognitive function follows an inverted U-shape function.
source: Several studies have shown that effects of dopaminergic drugs on cognitive function depend on an individual's baseline level of performance or dopamine activity reviewed in Cools and D'Esposito, 2011, Frank and Fossella, 2011, consistent with the idea that the relationship between dopamine activity and neurocognitive function follows an inverted U-shape function (Cools and Robbins, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drug effects on prediction-error-related dopamine and/or opioid activity may not always produce corresponding changes in the BOLD signal.
source: Finally, it is important to note that drug effects on prediction-error-related dopamine and/or opioid activity may not always produce corresponding changes in the BOLD signal (Knutson and Gibbs, 2007; Brocka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One study reported an increased reward prediction-error signal in a levodopa group compared to a haloperidol group (although neither of these groups differed from a placebo group).
source: One study reported an increased reward prediction-error signal in an levodopa group compared to a haloperidol group (although neither of these groups differed from a placebo group) (Pessiglione et al., 2006), but two recent studies using within-subject designs found no levodopa effects on neural reward prediction-error signals (Kroemer et al., 2019; Chakroun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous research.

claim: Two recent studies using within-subject designs found no levodopa effects on neural reward prediction-error signals.
source: One study reported an increased reward prediction-error signal in an levodopa group compared to a haloperidol group (although neither of these groups differed from a placebo group) (Pessiglione et al., 2006), but two recent studies using within-subject designs found no levodopa effects on neural reward prediction-error signals (Kroemer et al., 2019; Chakroun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous research.

claim: A lack of statistical power due to moderate sample size and between-subject design may have prevented the detection of drug effects in the fMRI analyses.
source: As mentioned above, a lack of statistical power due to our moderate sample size and between-subject design may have prevented the detection of drug effects in our fMRI analyses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the null fMRI findings.

claim: The drug effects on learning parameters in the present study suggest that the pharmacological interventions were effective.
source: Our drug doses were based on previous pharmacological studies with between-subject designs which reported significant drug effects (Pessiglione et al., 2006; Eippert et al., 2008; Guitart-Masip et al., 2012; Oei et al., 2012; Beierholm et al., 2013; Bunzeck et al., 2014; Guitart-Masip et al., 2014; Wittmann and D'Esposito, 2015), and the drug effects on learning parameters in the present study suggests that our pharmacological interventions were effective as well.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed drug effects on learning rates.

claim: Given the absence of a manipulation check, it is unknown whether the null findings are due to a true lack of dopaminergic/opioidergic regulation of pain-avoidance learning, an ineffectiveness of the pharmacological manipulations, or a lack of statistical power.
source: However, given the absence of a manipulation check, it is unknown whether our null findings are due to a true lack of dopaminergic/opioidergic regulation of pain-avoidance learning, an ineffectiveness of our pharmacological manipulations (e.g., because the doses were too low), or a lack of statistical power.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the study in interpreting the null findings.

claim: The absence of drug effects on fMRI results and model-independent performance measures should be taken with caution.
source: Thus, the absence of drug effects on our fMRI results and model-independent performance measures should be taken with caution.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpreting the null findings.

claim: It is unlikely that naltrexone affected participants' pain sensitivity because there were no effects of naltrexone on pain ratings immediately prior to the learning task.
source: However, we believe that it is unlikely that naltrexone affected participants' pain sensitivity because (1) we found no effects of naltrexone on pain ratings immediately prior to the learning task, and (2) previous studies suggest that opioid antagonists rarely affect pain perception in experimental pain paradigms (Grevert and Goldstein, 1977; Eippert et al., 2008; Werner et al., 2015; Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the null effect of naltrexone on pain ratings, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies suggest that opioid antagonists rarely affect pain perception in experimental pain paradigms.
source: However, we believe that it is unlikely that naltrexone affected participants' pain sensitivity because (1) we found no effects of naltrexone on pain ratings immediately prior to the learning task, and (2) previous studies suggest that opioid antagonists rarely affect pain perception in experimental pain paradigms (Grevert and Goldstein, 1977; Eippert et al., 2008; Werner et al., 2015; Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The fMRI data suffered from signal dropout in inferior parts of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex), which is a common problem in fMRI studies using echo-planar imaging.
source: Our fMRI data suffered from signal dropout in inferior parts of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex), which is a common problem in fMRI studies using echo-planar imaging (Ojemann et al., 1997; Deichmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a limitation of the fMRI data, with citations to previous work describing this issue.

claim: The results are agnostic with respect to the contribution of ventral prefrontal areas to pain-avoidance learning, and their potential modulation by levodopa or naltrexone.
source: Therefore, our results are agnostic with respect to the contribution of ventral prefrontal areas to pain-avoidance learning, and their potential modulation by levodopa or naltrexone.
evidence: This is an inference from the signal dropout limitation.

claim: Physiological data were not collected during fMRI scanning; hence could not remove potential artifacts related to cardiac and respiratory processes.
source: In addition, we did not collect physiological data during fMRI scanning; hence could not remove potential artifacts related to cardiac and respiratory processes.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the fMRI data collection.

claim: Correcting for physiological noise may have resulted in a higher signal-to-noise ratio and hence increase the significance of the results, especially in brainstem regions.
source: Correcting for physiological noise may have resulted in a higher signal-to-noise ratio and hence increase the significance of the results, especially in brainstem regions (Linnman et al., 2012; Brooks et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the limitation, with citations to previous work.

claim: It is unlikely that physiological noise was synchronized with the experimental design and thereby produced 'false positive' fMRI results.
source: Importantly, it is unlikely that physiological noise was synchronized with our experimental design (e.g., the application of pain outcomes) and thereby produced 'false positive' fMRI results because (1) frequencies of cardiac and respiration cycles are much higher than the frequency of our pain outcomes, and (2) we used jittered interstimulus intervals.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of the limitation on the validity of the results.

claim: Even if physiological changes in respiratory and cardiac cycle did correlate with the timing of pain outcomes, this would be unlikely to systematically affect prediction-error signals as these were based on parametric-modulator regressors that were orthogonal to the main outcome-onset regressors.
source: Furthermore, even if physiological changes in respiratory and cardiac cycle did correlate with the timing of our pain outcomes, this would be unlikely to systematically affect our prediction-error signals as these were based on parametric-modulator regressors that were orthogonal to the main outcome-onset regressors.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of the limitation on the validity of the results.

claim: Other neuromodulators are almost certainly involved in pain-avoidance learning as well.
source: Finally, regarding the role of neuromodulators, we focused on dopamine and endogenous opioids, but other neuromodulators are almost certainly involved in pain-avoidance learning as well.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader context of neuromodulatory involvement.

claim: Future work may focus on the serotonergic system, which has traditionally been associated with aversive processing, behavioral inhibition, and 'fight or flight' responses in rodents.
source: In particular, future work may focus on the serotonergic system, which has traditionally been associated with aversive processing, behavioral inhibition, and 'fight or flight' responses in rodents (Deakin, 1983; Soubrié, 1986, Deakin and Graeff, 1991).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research, with citations to previous work.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic studies have provided evidence for a role of the human serotonergic system in various aspects of aversive learning.
source: More recent pharmacological and genetic studies, which mostly used tasks with secondary reinforcers, have provided evidence for a role of the human serotonergic system in various aspects of aversive learning (Chamberlain et al., 2006; Cools et al., 2008; Crockett et al., 2012; Hindi Attar et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2012; den Ouden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It has been proposed that serotonin acts as an opponent to dopamine by mediating behavioral inhibition in response to punishment.
source: Based on these findings, it has been proposed that serotonin acts as an opponent to dopamine by mediating behavioral inhibition in response to punishment (Daw et al., 2002; Dayan and Huys, 2009; Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Cools et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Other studies have found effects of serotonin manipulations on both reward and punishment learning.
source: However, other studies have found effects of serotonin manipulations on both reward and punishment learning (Palminteri et al., 2012; Guitart-Masip et al., 2014), and a study in which participants simultaneously learned probabilities of monetary rewards and painful shocks suggested that serotonin selectively modulates reward processing (Seymour et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous research.

claim: A study in which participants simultaneously learned probabilities of monetary rewards and painful shocks suggested that serotonin selectively modulates reward processing.
source: However, other studies have found effects of serotonin manipulations on both reward and punishment learning (Palminteri et al., 2012; Guitart-Masip et al., 2014), and a study in which participants simultaneously learned probabilities of monetary rewards and painful shocks suggested that serotonin selectively modulates reward processing (Seymour et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous research.

claim: Previous work suggests that the serotonergic system has highly intricate and multifaceted roles in affective learning, likely due to its large number of receptor types, widespread projections, and interactions with other neuromodulators.
source: Taken together, previous work suggests that the serotonergic system has highly intricate and multifaceted roles in affective learning, likely due to its large number of receptor types, widespread projections, and interactions with other neuromodulators (Dayan and Huys, 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research with citation support.

claim: Future studies are required to further clarify the functional role(s) of serotonin in pain-avoidance learning.
source: Future studies are required to further clarify the functional role(s) of serotonin in pain-avoidance learning.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The computational-modeling results provide evidence for a causal role of the dopamine and endogenous opioid systems in learning from avoided, but not received, pain.
source: In sum, our results suggest that received and avoided pain drive human pain-avoidance learning via two different learning systems, in terms of both learning rates and the neural encoding of prediction errors. In addition, our computational-modeling results provide evidence for a causal role of the dopamine and endogenous opioid systems in learning from avoided, but not received, pain.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Future studies are needed to elucidate the neural mechanisms via which dopamine and opioid manipulations affected learning rates for avoided pain.
source: Future studies are needed to elucidate the neural mechanisms via which our dopamine and opioid manipulations affected learning rates for avoided pain, and to reveal the potential role of other neuromodulators in pain-avoidance learning.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Future studies are needed to reveal the potential role of other neuromodulators in pain-avoidance learning.
source: Future studies are needed to elucidate the neural mechanisms via which our dopamine and opioid manipulations affected learning rates for avoided pain, and to reveal the potential role of other neuromodulators in pain-avoidance learning.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Ninety-one healthy students (18–26 years old; 71% female; all right handed) took part in the study.
source: Ninety-one healthy students (18–26 years old; 71% female; all right handed) took part in the study.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Participants reported no history of psychiatric, neurological, or pain disorders, and no current pain.
source: Participants reported no history of psychiatric, neurological, or pain disorders, and no current pain.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study sample.

claim: The study was approved by the medical ethics committee of the Leiden University Medical Center (P15.116).
source: The study was approved by the medical ethics committee of the Leiden University Medical Center (P15.116), and all participants provided written informed consent.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the medical ethics committee of the Leiden University Medical Center (P15.116), and all participants provided written informed consent.
evidence: This describes the consent process for the study.

claim: Six participants were excluded from all analyses because of thermode failure.
source: Six participants were excluded from all analyses because of thermode failure, and two additional participants because of poor task performance (see 'Pain-avoidance learning task').
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the analyses.

claim: Two additional participants were excluded from all analyses because of poor task performance.
source: Six participants were excluded from all analyses because of thermode failure, and two additional participants because of poor task performance (see 'Pain-avoidance learning task').
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the analyses.

claim: Each eligible participant took part in one fMRI session.
source: Each eligible participant took part in one fMRI session.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: On the day of the fMRI session, participants received a single oral dose of either 100 mg levodopa, 50 mg naltrexone, or placebo, according to a double-blind, randomized, between-subject design.
source: On the day of the fMRI session, participants received a single oral dose of either 100 mg levodopa, 50 mg naltrexone, or placebo, according to a double-blind, randomized, between-subject design.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Levodopa was combined with 25 mg carbidopa—a decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood–brain barrier—to inhibit the conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the periphery.
source: Levodopa was combined with 25 mg carbidopa—a decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood–brain barrier—to inhibit the conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the periphery.
evidence: This describes the drug administration procedure.

claim: Approximately 30 min after drug administration, participants were positioned in the MRI scanner, after which a high-resolution structural scan was acquired.
source: Approximately 30 min after drug administration, participants were positioned in the MRI scanner, after which we acquired a high-resolution structural scan.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Approximately 53 min after drug administration, participants completed a 5-min pain-rating task during which they received a series of (unavoidable) heat stimuli of varying temperatures and rated their experienced pain following each stimulus.
source: Approximately 53 min after drug administration, participants completed a 5-min pain-rating task during which they received a series of (unavoidable) heat stimuli of varying temperatures and rated their experienced pain following each stimulus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sixty minutes after drug administration, roughly corresponding with peak plasma concentrations of levodopa and naltrexone, participants started the pain-avoidance learning task.
source: Sixty minutes after drug administration, roughly corresponding with peak plasma concentrations of levodopa and naltrexone, participants started the pain-avoidance learning task (described below), which lasted approximately 45 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and timing.

claim: The pain-avoidance learning task lasted approximately 45 min.
source: Sixty minutes after drug administration, roughly corresponding with peak plasma concentrations of levodopa and naltrexone, participants started the pain-avoidance learning task (described below), which lasted approximately 45 min.
evidence: This describes the duration of the task.

claim: Following the pain-avoidance learning task, participants performed an 8-min probabilistic reward-learning task (not reported here).
source: Following the pain-avoidance learning task, participants performed an 8-min probabilistic reward-learning task (not reported here).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjective state was measured at the beginning (before drug administration) and end (2 hr after drug administration) of the test session, by means of visual analog scales measuring alertness, calmness, and contentment.
source: We measured participants' subjective state at the beginning (before drug administration) and end (2 hr after drug administration) of the test session, by means of visual analog scales measuring alertness, calmness, and contentment (Bond and Lader, 1974 Bond and Lader, 1974; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the measurement of subjective state, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The instrumental pain-avoidance learning task contained 144 trials, divided in 4 runs of 36 trials.
source: This instrumental pain-avoidance learning task contained 144 trials, divided in 4 runs of 36 trials.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Three different pairs of random walks were used; each pair was administered to approximately one-third of the participants in each treatment group.
source: We used three different pairs of random walks (each pair crossed at least once); each pair was administered to approximately one-third of the participants in each treatment group.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Each trial started with the presentation of the two choice options, randomly displayed at the left and right side of the screen for 1800 ms.
source: Each trial started with the presentation of the two choice options, randomly displayed at the left and right side of the screen for 1800 ms (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the trial structure, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: If participants did not respond in time, the computer randomly selected an option for them (1.2% of trials).
source: If participants did not respond in time (1.2% of trials), the computer randomly selected an option for them.
evidence: This describes the task procedure and provides a descriptive statistic.

claim: Heat stimuli were applied to the inner side of participants' left lower leg using a Contact Heat-Evoked Potential Stimulator (CHEPS; 27 mm diameter Peltier thermode; Medoc Ltd., Israel).
source: Heat stimuli (ramp rate = 40°C/s; 1 s at target temperature) were applied to the inner side of participants' left lower leg using a Contact Heat-Evoked Potential Stimulator (CHEPS; 27 mm diameter Peltier thermode; Medoc Ltd., Israel).
evidence: This describes the thermal stimulation equipment and procedure.

claim: After the initial pain-rating task, 16% of the participants indicated that they would not tolerate repeated stimulation at the highest temperature they had received so far (50°C).
source: After the initial pain-rating task, 16% of the participants (four in the placebo, four in the levodopa, and seven in the naltrexone group) indicated that they would not tolerate repeated stimulation at the highest temperature they had received so far (50°C).
evidence: This describes the temperature selection procedure and provides a descriptive statistic.

claim: For participants who would not tolerate 50°C, a temperature of 49°C was used in the pain-avoidance learning task.
source: For those participants, we used a temperature of 49°C in the pain-avoidance learning task.
evidence: This describes the temperature selection procedure.

claim: For the remaining participants, a temperature of 50°C was used in the pain-avoidance learning task.
source: For the remaining participants, we used a temperature of 50°C.
evidence: This describes the temperature selection procedure.

claim: Two reinforcement-learning (Q learning) models were fitted to participants' choice data: one model with a single learning rate (Model 1), and one model with separate learning rates for pain and no-pain outcomes (Model 2).
source: We fitted two reinforcement-learning (Q learning) models to participants' choice data: one model with a single learning rate (Model 1), and one model with separate learning rates for pain and no-pain outcomes (Model 2).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach.

claim: The model parameters were estimated with a hierarchical Bayesian approach, using the hBayesDM package.
source: We estimated the model parameters with a hierarchical Bayesian approach, using the hBayesDM package (Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the parameter estimation method, with citation.

claim: Separate group-level parameters were estimated for the placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone groups.
source: We estimated separate group-level parameters for the placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone groups.
evidence: This describes the parameter estimation approach.

claim: Four independent MCMC chains with different starting values were run, which each generated 5000 posterior samples.
source: We ran 4 independent MCMC chains with different starting values, which each generated 5000 posterior samples.
evidence: This describes the MCMC sampling procedure.

claim: The first 1000 iterations of each chain were discarded as burn-in.
source: We discarded the first 1000 iterations of each chain as burn-in.
evidence: This describes the MCMC sampling procedure.

claim: Only every fifth iteration was used to remove autocorrelation.
source: In addition, we only used every fifth iteration to remove autocorrelation.
evidence: This describes the MCMC sampling procedure.

claim: 3200 representative samples (800 per chain) per parameter per model fit were obtained.
source: Consequently, we obtained 3200 representative samples (800 per chain) per parameter per model fit.
evidence: This describes the MCMC sampling procedure.

claim: All chains converged (Rhat values <1.1).
source: All chains converged (Rhat values <1.1).
evidence: This describes the convergence of the MCMC sampling.

claim: The two models were compared using the WAIC.
source: We compared the fit of our two models using the WAIC (Watanabe, 2010).
evidence: This describes the model comparison method, with citation.

claim: The WAIC provides an estimate of a model's out-of-sample predictive accuracy, adjusted for the number of free parameters, in a fully Bayesian way.
source: The WAIC provides an estimate of a model's out-of-sample predictive accuracy, adjusted for the number of free parameters, in a fully Bayesian way.
evidence: This describes the properties of the WAIC metric.

claim: Lower WAIC values indicate better out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
source: Lower WAIC values indicate better out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the WAIC metric.

claim: Trial-specific expected pain probabilities were computed by applying the winning model to each participant's sequence of choices and outcomes.
source: We computed trial-specific expected pain probabilities—to be used as parametric modulator regressors in the fMRI analyses—by applying our winning model to each participant's sequence of choices and outcomes.
evidence: This describes the computation of fMRI regressors.

claim: The exact same model was used to generate fMRI regressors for all participants by instantiating the model with the mean learning-rate parameters (the individual-level posterior medians, averaged across all participants).
source: In line with previous studies (Pine et al., 2010; Voon et al., 2010; Seymour et al., 2012; Hauser et al., 2015; Kroemer et al., 2019), we used the exact same model to generate fMRI regressors for all participants by instantiating the model with the mean learning-rate parameters (the individual-level posterior medians, averaged across all participants).
evidence: This describes the computation of fMRI regressors, with citations to previous work using similar approaches.
